articles.body: Tanker On Fire After Struck By Projectile Near Strait of Hormuz Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/IbrahimAlkan A tanker caught fire after being struck by an unknown projectile while sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Friday. The British navy-affiliated agency UKMTO said that the incident occurred 8 nautical miles north of the Omani town of Khasab, adding that no casualties or environmental impact were reported. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said shortly afterwards that an oil tanker had caught fire after hitting a mine while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz near Khasab, Iranian state media reported. Khasab lies on Oman's Musandam Peninsula at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway that carried nearly one-fifth of global crude oil supplies before the US-Israeli conflict with Iran. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted since Iran moved to close the waterway following the eruption of the conflict on February 28. (Reuters)

articles.title: Oil Prices Drop for Third Week Straight
articles.summary: Oil prices fell on Friday and were set for a weekly decline on strong exports from the Middle East despite Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.Brent crude futures were down 67 cents, or 0.7%, at $91.31 a barrel at 1414 GMT.
articles.body: Oil Prices Drop for Third Week Straight Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Zulfugar Karimov Oil prices fell on Friday and were set for a weekly decline on strong exports from the Middle East despite Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures were down 67 cents, or 0.7%, at $91.31 a barrel at 1414 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate futures for December were down 36 cents, or 0.4%, at $82.85 a barrel, while the more active January contract was down 19 cents, or 0.2%, at $82.85. Brent is on track for a near 5% decline for the week and the December WTI contract for a 6.5% weekly drop as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. This would be the benchmarks' third straight week of decline. "This week we keep having relatively strong export flows out of the Middle East. There is also a narrative ongoing that as long as people are talking, maybe there's a deal in the making," said Aldo Spanjer, commodity strategist at BNP Paribas. "The prices are correct if you believe that this geopolitical risk doesn't come back. I'm not in that camp who thinks this is done ... I probably see a rebound," he said. On Friday, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement warned workers and people near Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports to evacuate immediately and urged shipping companies to remove vessels, saying they would target Saudi ports in Jeddah and the Red Sea if a Saudi-led coalition strikes Yemen's Hodeidah port. The Houthis fired missiles at Riyadh on Thursday. Two oil tankers also hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and "are burning," Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by state media on Thursday. Iran's intensifying attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, "running at roughly one incident per day in November," still add a meaningful geopolitical risk premium to the market, according to UOB Group analysts in a client note. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia. The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency said on Thursday. However, some analysts expect softness in the broader equities markets to weigh on oil prices, as Asian shares fell on Friday — heading for their worst week since 2020. "Supply disruptions remain a risk, but near-term demand concerns tied to the AI trade unwind and broader risk-off sentiment are weighing on prices," said Saxo analysts in a note. In Russia, crude oil output could fall again as Ukrainian attacks on refineries and export infrastructure intensify, analysts and traders say. Ukrainian drone a ttacks have cut Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, Reuters reported on Wednesday. (Reuters)

articles.body: Baltic Exchange welcomes new Lord Mayor of the City of London in International Shipping News 20/11/2026 Baltic Exchange is delighted to welcome Alderman Bronek Masojada as the newly elected and 698th Lord Mayor of the City of London. He succeeded Lady Mayor Dame Susan Langley DBE on 13 November at the Silent Ceremony at Guildhall, which was followed by the annual Lord Mayor’s Show in the City of London the next day. The Lord Mayor spent 28 years at insurance giant Hiscox, including 21 years as Group Chief Executive, helping transform it into a leading global specialist insurer. He has also held senior roles across the insurance market and is Chair of the East End Community Foundation, supporting work to improve life chances and employment prospects across East London. The Lord Mayor also sits on the London International Shipping Week Board of Advisors. As Lord Mayor, Bronek will act as an international ambassador for the UK’s financial and professional services sector, championing its contribution to prosperity at home and abroad, as well as the UK’s role as a trusted partner that connects markets, nations, and ideas. This includes promoting London’s rich maritime heritage and its pivotal role in global finance, as well as the Baltic Exchange’s own role in supporting international shipping markets from its historic foundations at the heart of London’s maritime community. The Baltic looks forward to hosting a lunch in honour of the new Lord Mayor in December. On behalf of the international shipping community, the Baltic Exchange is delighted to welcome the Lord Mayor to his new role and looks forward to working closely with him and fellow shipping leaders to champion London’s place at the centre of the international maritime sector. articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said it had struck the Red Sea port of Hodeidah to destroy Houthi capabilities on Friday, as the militants warned airlines to avoid Saudi airspace, pledging new air strikes within hours.The developments…
articles.body: Saudi Forces Strike Hodeidah Port as Houthis Warn Airlines Away From Airspace Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © AU USAnakul / Adobe Stock The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said it had struck the Red Sea port of Hodeidah to destroy Houthi capabilities on Friday, as the militants warned airlines to avoid Saudi airspace, pledging new air strikes within hours. The developments, a day after the group struck the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh, signalled a worsening of a conflict that has brought a humanitarian crisis to Yemen and severe disruption to Saudi Arabia, in parallel with the US-led war against Iran. Hodeidah is the main port bringing food and other supplies into Houthi-controlled northern Yemen. The coalition had earlier warned civilians to evacuate the area. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed operational capabilities at the port that were used in smuggling operations and the transport of weapons and ballistic missiles. The port remains fully operational and the flow of goods will continue, according to Yemen’s Information Minister. HOUTHIS TELL SHIPPING COMPANIES TO EVACUATE FROM SAUDI PORTS There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, who had earlier said they would hit Red Sea ports if the Saudis carried out their own threat to strike the Yemeni port. "We warn all employees, workers, and those in the vicinity of (Saudi Arabia's Red Sea) ports to evacuate them immediately and stay away. We also urge all shipping companies to immediately evacuate their ships from these ports," Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement. Airlines should avoid Saudi airspace "because it will be the scene of our operations in the coming hours," Saree said, making an exception for airspace near the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina. He also said the group would target a power station at Shuqaiq in southern Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led coalition also said it carried out an operation in Yemen's capital Sanaa targeting ballistic missile and drone capabilities and that operations in Saada and Taiz were ongoing. Since fighting resumed in Yemen in July in parallel with the wider Iran war, the Houthis have rapidly advanced in Yemen, seizing territory from Yemen's internationally recognised government and its allies, who are backed by Saudi Arabia. The Saudis have carried out air strikes on Yemen in support of their allies on the ground, while the Houthis have struck Saudi oil targets, airports and office towers. Deadly strikes on Riyadh's main airport last month led to the cancellation of most international flights, and Saudi Arabia has postponed or cancelled high-profile global events including soccer's AFC Asian Cup. Saudi Arabia, a close ally of the United States, has been backing Yemen's internationally recognised government for more than a decade in a war that was fought to a stalemate in 2022 but reignited in July this year. The Houthis have seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and forced the Saudi-backed forces aligned with the government to retreat over the weekend to defend their temporary capital in the southern port of Aden. (Reuters)

articles.summary: DP World has announced an expanded investment of US$ 200 million in the Port of Maputo, following a meeting between Group Executive Chairman H.E. articles.body: DP World has announced an expanded investment of US$ 200 million in the Port of Maputo, following a meeting between Group Executive Chairman H.E. Essa Kazim and Mozambique’s President, H.E. Daniel Chapo. The figure raises the company’s original commitment of USD 165 million and supports its ambition to strengthen Mozambique’s position as a strategic trade and logistics gateway for Southern Africa. The meeting focused on expanding operations, exploring further investment in trade infrastructure and improving transport and logistics links with neighbouring markets. The expanded project will nearly triple the container terminal’s annual handling capacity, from 225,000 TEU to 650,000 TEU by the second quarter of 2027, exceeding the original target of 530,000 TEU. It will let the terminal accommodate larger vessels, improve operational efficiency and reinforce Maputo’s role as a regional logistics hub. DP World operates the Maputo container terminal and is a shareholder in the Maputo Port Development Company, which holds the port concession until 2058. Beyond the port, Maputo is emerging as a multimodal gateway linking Southern Africa’s industrial and agricultural heartlands to global markets, and DP World is strengthening these connections through cross-border road and rail networks and its inland logistics hub at Komatipoort in South Africa. Its Shipping Solutions business is also due to launch a new weekly China-Africa Link later this month, connecting Shanghai, Ningbo, Nansha and other Chinese ports with Maputo and other regional gateways, which together will make the Maputo Corridor a more competitive route for regional trade. Essa Kazim said Mozambique has an opportunity to become one of Southern Africa’s most important trade gateways, and that the ambition is not simply to move more cargo through Maputo but to connect businesses across the region to global markets through better infrastructure, shipping services and inland logistics, helping Mozambique capture more of the value of regional trade.

articles.summary: Another tanker was struck by a projectile and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, extending a wave of attacks on commercial shipping that has pushed maritime security...

REUTERS/Stringer Another tanker was struck by a projectile and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, extending a wave of attacks on commercial shipping that has pushed maritime security incidents to their highest weekly level since mid-October. The latest incident occurred at approximately 1500 UTC, eight nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Warning 214-26 . The tanker was transiting outbound through the strategic waterway when an unknown projectile struck its port bow, sparking a fire onboard. The vessel’s company security officer reported no casualties or environmental impact. Authorities are investigating. The attack comes amid a sharp escalation in threats to merchant shipping across the Middle East and Black Sea. According to maritime security analyst Martin Kelly of Orbital Risk Intelligence, shipping experienced 15 attacks and piracy-related incidents over the past seven days, a 50% increase from the previous week and the highest weekly total since mid-October. In the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, Kelly recorded seven strikes involving six vessels. Four tankers were hit within 13 nautical miles of Khasab over three days, including the LPG tanker TARA GAS , which was attacked twice. The violence has left two seafarers missing and 13 injured, according to Kelly’s assessment. Among the most serious incidents was the November 17 attack on the tanker NAVIG8 MESSI , which suffered a fire after being struck 13 nautical miles north of Khasab. ADNOC confirmed that one crew member was missing and 11 others were injured. The remaining crew were evacuated and the vessel was reported under tow. The TARA GAS , meanwhile, was disabled by a projectile strike on November 16 before being hit again the following day, resulting in another fire and the vessel being abandoned. The pattern points to an increasingly dangerous concentration of attacks along the southern shipping lanes off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, particularly against tankers attempting to leave the Persian Gulf. The deteriorating security situation is taking a continued toll on commercial traffic. In its weekly maritime security overview published Friday , UKMTO reported 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits over the preceding seven days, down from 139 outbound and 169 inbound crossings the previous week. Combined traffic remains approximately 65% below pre-conflict levels. UKMTO recorded six verified attacks across the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf during its latest reporting period, which covered incidents through November 18. Four occurred in the Strait itself and two in the wider Persian Gulf. Two vessels required assistance, while the outcomes of four others remained unknown. The agency cautioned that its figures do not capture every incident, as some reports cannot be independently verified. Since the U.S.-Iran ceasefire agreement expired on August 17, UKMTO has recorded six total vessel losses, while 22 vessels required assistance and 31 were confirmed to have continued their voyages. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) continues to assess the threat to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz as SEVERE , warning that further deliberate attacks are highly likely. The surge in maritime violence extends well beyond the Middle East. Six commercial vessels were struck in the western Black Sea over the past week, according to Kelly, including two ships that sank in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone on consecutive days. The general cargo ship BETUL 8 sank on November 16, followed by the LPG tanker GAS HUSKY on November 17. All 31 seafarers aboard the two vessels were rescued. Maritime security firm Ambrey separately confirmed reports of six vessels struck since November 13, including four attacked near the Sulina anchorage in Romanian waters and two in Bulgarian waters. Ambrey assessed the attacks as part of an escalating Russian campaign involving unmanned aerial and surface vessels. The incidents have raised growing concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in waters adjacent to NATO member states Romania and Bulgaria. Piracy-related activity has also increased in the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. During the week, a tanker reported being approached by an armed skiff carrying a ladder approximately 430 nautical miles east of Socotra, Yemen. In another incident off Al Mukalla, armed guards aboard a cargo vessel fired a warning shot to repel an attempted boarding. The developments, a day after the group struck the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh, signaled a worsening of a conflict that has brought a humanitarian crisis to Yemen and severe disruption to Saudi Arabia, in parallel with the US-led war against Iran. Hodeidah is the main port bringing food and other supplies into Houthi-controlled northern Yemen. The coalition had earlier warned civilians to evacuate the area. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed operational capabilities at the port that were used in smuggling operations and the transport of weapons and ballistic missiles. Airlines should avoid Saudi airspace “because it will be the scene of our operations in the coming hours,” Saree said, making an exception for airspace near the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina. He also said the group would target a power station at Shuqaiq in southern Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led coalition also said it carried out an operation in Yemen’s capital Sanaa targeting ballistic missile and drone capabilities and that operations in Saada and Taiz were ongoing. Since fighting resumed in Yemen in July in parallel with the wider Iran war, the Houthis have rapidly advanced in Yemen, seizing territory from Yemen’s internationally recognized government and its allies, who are backed by Saudi Arabia. The Saudis have carried out air strikes on Yemen in support of their allies on the ground, while the Houthis have struck Saudi oil targets, airports and office towers. Deadly strikes on Riyadh’s main airport last month led to the cancellation of most international flights, and Saudi Arabia has postponed or canceled high-profile global events including soccer’s AFC Asian Cup. articles.summary: South Korean shipbuilder Samsung Heavy Industries and U.S. nuclear technology company Tesser Atomics have signed an exclusive agreement to develop a nuclear-powered LNG carrier intended for commercial service between the...

Join the leading maritime news network Illustration: Shutterstock South Korean shipbuilder Samsung Heavy Industries and U.S. nuclear technology company Tesser Atomics have signed an exclusive agreement to develop a nuclear-powered LNG carrier intended for commercial service between the United States and Europe. The memorandum of understanding, signed November 19, establishes Samsung Heavy Industries as the exclusive shipbuilding partner and Tesser Atomics as the exclusive reactor technology partner for the demonstration project, which aims to develop the world’s first nuclear-powered LNG carrier. The collaboration brings together Samsung’s ship design and construction capabilities with Tesser’s advanced reactor technology as the companies work toward demonstrating nuclear propulsion on an established commercial trade route. At the center of the project is Tesser’s Triton reactor, a compact fluoride-salt-cooled high-temperature reactor designed specifically for marine applications. The system uses TRISO nuclear fuel and low-pressure molten salt coolant, with a design that allows refueling while the reactor remains in operation. The companies say the technology could provide the power needed to propel large oceangoing vessels without relying on conventional marine fuels. “Demonstrating nuclear propulsion on an LNG carrier crossing the Atlantic would open new horizons for decarbonizing the shipping industry,” said Kyunghee Kim, Executive Vice President and Head of the Future Business Division at Samsung Heavy Industries. The project builds on Norway’s NuProShip research program, which evaluated advanced reactor technologies for merchant vessels, and is being advanced through SFI SAINT, a research consortium led by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) and supported by the Research Council of Norway. The Norwegian initiative is targeting several nuclear-powered vessel demonstrations in the early 2030s, including an LNG carrier project backed by shipowner Knutsen OAS. Samsung Heavy Industries is no stranger to nuclear-powered LNG carrier development. In September 2025, the shipbuilder and the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute secured Approval in Principle from ABS and the Liberian flag state for a separate LNG carrier concept powered by a 100-megawatt-thermal molten salt reactor. The latest agreement represents another step toward moving nuclear propulsion beyond conceptual designs and into commercial demonstration. However, significant hurdles remain. Nuclear-powered merchant ships face complex requirements involving reactor licensing, maritime safety, port access, crew training, insurance and liability. The International Maritime Organization is currently working to modernize its regulatory framework for nuclear-powered ships, with adoption of a revised Nuclear Code and amendments to SOLAS Chapter VIII targeted for 2030. The economics also remain uncertain. An ABS-supported study published in October found that a nuclear-powered LNG carrier could cost roughly 2.5 times as much to build as a conventional vessel, although lower fuel costs could improve its long-term economics. For now, the Samsung-Tesser agreement remains a development partnership rather than a firm shipbuilding order. The companies have not disclosed a construction schedule, vessel specifications, project cost or financing arrangements. Still, the project adds to growing efforts by shipbuilders, reactor developers and maritime regulators to determine whether nuclear propulsion can become a commercially viable alternative for deep-sea shipping. articles.summary: US Treasury Department officials met with government authorities in Singapore and Malaysia this week, including regulators and national security bodies, to warn of potential risks they could face if they do not comply with US sanctions on Iran.

REUTERS/Ints Kalnins SINGAPORE, Nov 20 (Reuters) – US Treasury Department officials met with government authorities in Singapore and Malaysia this week, including regulators and national security bodies, to warn of potential risks they could face if they do not comply with US sanctions on Iran. Washington is urging the countries, as well as law firms and banks operating there, to stay alert for Iranian front companies, as it steps up efforts to enforce sanctions in Asia and bring about a speedy end to the conflict in the Middle East. The US is urging additional scrutiny on “high-risk” sectors such as maritime transport, aviation services and procurement networks, “to make sure they’re not fronting for Iran,” said a Treasury Department official. “We want it to be understood too, that we’re going to target these lifelines, and it’s not going to be a negotiation when we find a lifeline that needs to be targeted,” the official said. Since the US and Israel commenced strikes on Iran in February, the US has intensified actions to throttle Tehran’s business interests overseas. In August, President Donald Trump’s administration launched Operation Economic Outcast, resulting in a barrage of sanctions against targets spanning Canadian digital currency platforms to a major Russian banking group. OIL ON WATER For years, tankers have regularly made stops in the waters around Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia to make ship-to-ship transfers of Iranian oil that help obscure its origin. Last year, Malaysian authorities said they would more tightly enforce rules around these transfers and in February seized two tankers and their cargoes. Since April, the US Navy has imposed a blockade on shipping reaching Iran through the Strait of Hormuz, and this month has cracked down on movement over Iran’s land borders and through the Caspian Sea. In July, the Treasury Department sanctioned dozens of individuals, vessels and companies based in Singapore, Hong Kong, the UAE, the Marshall Islands and St Kitts and Nevis linked to Iranian oil magnate Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani. These efforts were starting to disrupt Iran’s source of revenue, the US official said, citing data showing that the country is currently undergoing the worst GDP contraction in four decades and the highest rate of inflation since World War II. However, the official said there was still work to be done. “There’s an Iranian airline that flies to Malaysia, or has, recently, so we raised this,” the US official said, without naming the carrier. Using public flight records, Reuters identified a regularly scheduled flight between Tehran and Kuala Lumpur operated by Iran Airtour, which flew as recently as November 14. A scheduled flight on November 17 did not depart, the records also show. Iran Airtour did not respond to an emailed request for comment sent outside of business hours on Friday. Most Iranian airlines largely stopped flying to Malaysia in 2022 due to US sanctions on refueling Iranian planes. However, Iran Airtour, a privately owned airline, resumed flights to Malaysia in November 2025, according to Iranian media. On September 8, the US imposed sanctions on dozens of companies in the UAE, Britain, Malaysia, Turkey and Kazakhstan it said were supporting Iran’s aviation sector to move weapons, personnel and illicit cargo. The following day, Iran Air officials met with Malaysia’s ambassador to Iran to discuss resuming direct flights between Iran and Kuala Lumpur. Both Malaysia and Singapore implement UN Security Council sanctions on Iran. Singapore’s government said in a statement it “is firmly committed to doing our part” and “preventing bad actors from abusing our corporate vehicles,” citing its efforts to strengthen vigilance in the maritime and financial industries this year. The Malaysian government did not respond to requests for comment. Image courtesy Carnival Corporation Carnival Corporation has signed a contract with Italian shipbuilding giant Fincantieri for two next-generation cruise ships, marking a shift toward smaller vessels designed to reach more destinations. The agreement, valued at more than €2 billion ($2.2 billion), calls for construction of two dual-fuel cruise ships at Fincantieri’s Marghera shipyard in Italy, with deliveries scheduled for 2033 and 2035. Each vessel will measure approximately 130,000 gross tons and feature around 1,650 passenger cabins. The ships will primarily operate on liquefied natural gas (LNG) and incorporate advanced environmental and digital technologies. Unlike Carnival’s recent focus on increasingly massive cruise ships, the new class is being designed with greater operational flexibility in mind, allowing the company to serve ports and destinations that may be inaccessible to its largest vessels. Carnival Cruise Line President Christine Duffy said the new ships will complement the company’s existing fleet of 29 vessels. “With a 29-ship fleet, we know our guests appreciate choices,” Duffy said. “They love the incredible experiences and amenities on our Excel Class ships, the largest in our fleet, but they also love the intimacy our smaller ships offer.” Fincantieri said the design has also been developed as a multi-brand platform, potentially allowing Carnival Corporation to adopt the same basic vessel design across several of its cruise lines in the future. articles.title: IMO Finds Just $10.5 Billion in Maritime Climate Finance
articles.summary: A new study by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has identified just $10.5 billion in direct maritime climate finance over a six-year period, accounting for only 0.14% of global climate...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network FILE PHOTO: By Mr Nai / Shutterstock A new study by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has identified just $10.5 billion in direct maritime climate finance over a six-year period, accounting for only 0.14% of global climate finance flows, highlighting a significant funding gap as the shipping industry faces mounting pressure to decarbonize. The findings, released Thursday , come from the IMO’s Maritime Climate Finance Landscape report, which tracked investment between 2018 and 2023 across shipping, ports, alternative fuels and other maritime activities. The study, developed in collaboration with Climate Policy Initiative under the IMO’s GHG-SMART Programme, found that maritime climate finance has grown substantially but remains far below the investment needed to meet the industry’s long-term emissions targets. Annual financing reached $4.7 billion in 2023, representing a compound annual growth rate of 49% over the study period. However, much of that growth was driven by a relatively small number of large projects, raising questions about whether the increases can be sustained. The report estimates that decarbonizing international shipping and developing the supporting shore-based infrastructure will require between $1.2 trillion and $1.6 trillion in capital investment by 2050. The study found that most tracked climate finance flowed into port infrastructure and alternative fuel production, while investments in vessel technologies, shipbuilding and recycling received considerably less attention. In 2023 alone, alternative fuel production and distribution attracted $2.5 billion, while port infrastructure and operations received $1.4 billion. Together, those two categories accounted for approximately 83% of direct maritime climate finance that year. Across the full six-year period, port infrastructure accounted for 39% of tracked financing, followed by alternative fuel production and distribution at 24%. Maritime operations and technologies received 11%, while shipbuilding and recycling accounted for just 0.02%. Public and private investors contributed roughly comparable amounts, although commercial debt dominated the financing landscape, accounting for 61% of tracked flows. Grants represented just 12%. The findings underscore a central challenge facing shipping’s energy transition: investments in cleaner vessels, alternative fuel production and port infrastructure must move forward together. Shipowners need confidence that alternative fuels will be available before committing to new vessels, while fuel producers and ports need assurances that sufficient demand will exist to justify major infrastructure investments. The report also highlights significant disparities in access to maritime climate finance, particularly among small island developing states (SIDS) and least developed countries (LDCs). Although those countries received approximately 68% of tracked maritime climate adaptation finance between 2018 and 2023, primarily for port resilience projects, they accounted for just 1.5% of maritime climate mitigation financing. Almost no tracked financing reached those countries for alternative fuel production and distribution, leaving them largely dependent on international public funding and concessional loans. The IMO said greater coordination between governments, financial institutions and industry will be necessary to improve access to capital, particularly in countries where maritime transport provides a critical link for trade, food, fuel and essential supplies. The study also acknowledged important limitations in the available data. Domestic public spending and private investment in ship retrofits, energy efficiency and shipbuilding are not consistently captured, meaning the $10.5 billion figure should not be interpreted as a complete accounting of all maritime decarbonization investment. The IMO called for more consistent definitions of maritime climate finance, stronger reporting systems and better coordination of investment-ready projects to help direct additional funding into the sector. A Maltese-flagged bulk carrier ran aground on France’s Atlantic coast early Friday after being driven toward shore by strong winds and heavy seas, prompting the helicopter evacuation of 19 crew members and a major maritime emergency response. The 169-meter MIRO G grounded near Lit-et-Mixe in southwestern France’s Landes region shortly after midnight on November 20, after its crew reported difficulty maneuvering in deteriorating weather. According to France’s Atlantic Maritime Prefecture, the vessel alerted the CROSS-A Étel rescue coordination center Thursday evening after encountering heavy swell and strong crosswinds. The crew attempted an emergency anchorage, but wind gusts reaching 48 knots caused the vessel to drag anchor and drift toward shore. Following the grounding, a French Air and Space Force search-and-rescue helicopter operating from Cazaux evacuated 19 of the vessel’s 22 crew members. The captain and two other mariners remained aboard to assist authorities with the ongoing response. French authorities have since shifted their attention to the possibility of refloating the vessel. A French Navy evaluation and intervention team was deployed by helicopter to assess the ship’s condition and determine whether it can be safely pulled free. Meanwhile, the emergency towing vessel Abeille Bretagne departed Brest in anticipation of a possible refloating operation. A French Navy Falcon 50 maritime surveillance aircraft has also been monitoring the grounded vessel. Authorities said its initial aerial assessment found no evidence of pollution. However, the operation faces significant challenges. According to AFP, the vessel is carrying more than 100 tonnes of diesel fuel, presenting a potential pollution risk. French maritime officials said options under consideration include pumping fuel from the vessel to reduce its weight before attempting to tow it into deeper water. The operation is complicated by rough weather, including waves reaching five to six meters, and difficult access to the beach. The MIRO G , a 2011-built Handysize bulk carrier with a deadweight capacity of approximately 28,200 tonnes, was sailing without cargo when the grounding occurred. The ship was reportedly bound for Rouen, France, where it was scheduled to load approximately 30,000 tonnes of wheat destined for Libya. The incident triggered the activation of Level 3 of France’s ORSEC maritime emergency response system, as well as the Franco-Spanish Biscaye Plan, a bilateral agreement coordinating maritime rescue and pollution response in the Bay of Biscay. The Spanish emergency towing vessel Sar Gavia was also mobilized under the agreement. French authorities have formally instructed the shipowner to take necessary measures to eliminate immediate and future dangers and minimize any potential environmental damage. As of Friday, no pollution had been detected, and the maritime prefecture said operations remained underway. November 20, 2026 © Dongara Marine The Cook Labor Government is investing $13.4 million in two new vessels to strengthen fisheries compliance and protect the Kimberley's valuable marine resources. A new nine-meter amphibious vessel is now operating out of Broome, undertaking patrols across the Buccaneer Archipelago Marine Park. The vessel was built by global business Sealegs who specialize in manufacturing the versatile craft. The vessel's ability to travel on both land and water will allow Fisheries and Marine Officers to access remote locations where extreme tidal conditions and limited boat ramp infrastructure can make launching traditional vessels difficult. The vessel will support joint patrols with local Aboriginal ranger groups, strengthening partnerships and supporting the shared management of the culturally significant region. The larger 22-meter patrol vessel will also be based in Broome, supporting commercial and recreational fisheries compliance and marine park management across northern waters. Expected to be delivered in October 2028, the new vessel will be built by Dongara Marine, providing another boost to Western Australia's marine manufacturing industry. The Geraldton business also delivered the new PV Equinox earlier this year, replacing the ageing PV Walcott and strengthening the State's fisheries patrol capabilities across the Kimberley.

articles.body: Hatenboer-Water Breaks Ground on New Headquarters in Schiedam Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © Hatenboer-Water Hatenboer-Water has started building a new headquarters in Schiedam, driving the first foundation pile on Thursday after early demolition work. Due to finish in the third quarter of 2027, the new building project adds manufacturing space and twice the company's current testing capacity as orders grow across shipping and offshore energy. Hatenboer-Water's existing premises in Schiedam have reached their limit. Rebuilding on site upgrades its engineering workshops and manufacturing facilities and keeps the business inside the Port of Rotterdam maritime cluster. Schiedam's focus on maritime manufacturing puts the company close to European shipbuilders, engineering firms and offshore service providers. The site also serves as the main hub for regional offices in Aberdeen, Dubai, Houston, Singapore and Hamburg. Doubling production and testing capacity means Hatenboer-Water can build more systems and run several demanding tests simultaneously, cutting waiting times and speeding up delivery. Inside, the building includes new production equipment, a better layout for moving materials, shared meeting spaces for visiting clients, and upgraded IT infrastructure and access controls. Separate, fully secured office zones with restricted access will let teams work on confidential projects. Designed as an all-electric, fully insulated building, it will also operate without natural gas. Daily operations will not stop during construction. Using a phased 'chessboard' plan, the existing building will stay in use while the first new sections are built. Staff and equipment will move across step by step as each part finishes, keeping production and support running as normal through 2027.

Azule Energy has completed the sale of its participating interests in blocks 14 and 14K offshore Angola to Etu Energias. The transaction comprises 20% participating interest in Block 14 and 10% participating interest in Block 14K, with the completion following the fulfilment of the applicable conditions and receipt of the required approvals. The company explains that this transaction supports the continued optimization of its portfolio and focus on strategic priorities, while reinforcing its long-term commitment to the country and its energy sector. We would like to thank our partners, RMB, the relevant authorities and all those involved in supporting a safe and orderly transition. articles.body: Vice Adm. Burdian appointed as DHS Joint Task Force-Maritime Director Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 Vice Adm. Jo‑Ann Burdian. Image courtesy USCG Vice Adm. Jo‑Ann Burdian was presidentially appointed as the director, Department of Homeland Security Joint Task Force–Maritime (JTF-M), effective Nov. 10, 2026. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin nominated Burdian as director of JTF-M, in accordance with 6 U.S.C. § 348(b)(3)(A), to ensure the critical, continued role of JTF-M in synchronizing multi-agency maritime operations and securing the nation’s maritime borders. “Vice Admiral Burdian’s appointment as the JTF-M director marks a pivotal moment for our collective maritime defense," said Mullin. "Her unmatched operational expertise is critical as JTF-M continues to dismantle illicit networks, prevent hostile exploitation of our maritime borders, and leverage the MOC-P construct to achieve departmental unity of effort and drive nationwide success." JTF-M synchronizes DHS component operations, intelligence, and investigations across the maritime domain to secure U.S. borders, prevent and respond to homeland security crises and facilitate regionally based joint operations. As the DHS Maritime Operations Coordination Plan (MOC-P) program office, JTF-M enhances coordination among DHS components, eliminating redundancy and increasing effectiveness through 35 Regional Coordinating Mechanisms (ReCoMs). These ReCoMs execute DHS missions at every major U.S. port, along all U.S. coastlines and approaches to maritime borders of the U.S. and its territories. The ReCoMs help prevent terrorist, criminal, and hostile activities and dismantle illicit networks attempting to exploit the maritime domain and reduce vulnerabilities while safeguarding legal trade and travel. "I am honored to lead the dedicated staff of Joint Task Force-Maritime as we strengthen our borders and streamline interagency response," said Burdian. "Through our 35 ReCoMs and strong partnerships with the Department of War, we will continue to safeguard legal trade and travel while remaining an impenetrable barrier against cross-border smuggling, illegal immigration and illicit trafficking." Burdian also serves as commander, Coast Guard Atlantic Area and commander, Coast Guard Defense Force East, providing Coast Guard forces and operations across all mission areas from the Arctic Ocean to the Arabian Gulf in support of the DoW and combatant commanders for national defense missions.

articles.title: Energy-Saving System for Marine Generators Touts 10% Fuel Savings
articles.summary: NYK Line, MTI Co., Oshima Shipbuilding, Terasaki Electric and Daihatsu Infinearth have verified the energy-saving performance and operational safety of the Hz Controller System, an energy-saving system for marine generators developed through joint testing.
articles.body: Energy-Saving System for Marine Generators Touts 10% Fuel Savings Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 Copyright Xavier MARCHANT/AdobeStock NYK Line, MTI Co., Oshima Shipbuilding, Terasaki Electric and Daihatsu Infinearth have verified the energy-saving performance and operational safety of the Hz Controller System, an energy-saving system for marine generators developed through joint testing. General sales of the system will now begin. Building on their joint research, the five companies will expand deployment beyond NYK-operated vessels, promoting installation on newbuildings and retrofitting on existing ships owned by other shipowners. The System reduces power consumption and generator fuel consumption by lowering the generator frequency while maintaining the performance required by onboard equipment. This is possible because onboard equipment such as pumps and motors that operate in conjunction with the power supply frequency is designed to deliver the required performance even under anticipated severe conditions and may therefore have excess capacity during normal navigation. Specifically, the System switches between the regular frequency and a lower energy-saving frequency according to shipboard conditions within the range specified by ship classification rules. It utilizes generator frequency control technology (Patent Number JP6238600) that is jointly patented by NYK and Tsuneishi Shipbuilding. Demonstration tests confirmed an approximately 10% reduction in generator fuel consumption compared with operation at the regular frequency. Subsequent verification on an increasing number of vessels equipped with the system confirmed a similar reduction. For general sales, Terasaki Electric will be responsible for the design and supply of the System, while Daihatsu Infinearth will expand its lineup of generator engines compatible with the System.

REUTERS/Stringer By Weilun Soon Nov 20, 2026 (Bloomberg) –A cargo of Iranian crude was transferred between two tankers in the Persian Gulf this week, as the US warned its navy could target vessels that carry out the practice while enforcing a maritime blockade. A US-sanctioned Suezmax called Olym transferred oil to the medium-range Hao Fan on Tuesday, according to nonprofit group United Against Nuclear Iran and data analytics platform Kpler. UANI said Hao Fan, which is not blacklisted by Washington, is spoofing its location near Oman’s Shinas. The tankers turned off their transponders during the operation, which UANI said took place just south of Iran’s main oil export terminal on Kharg Island, deep in the Persian Gulf. It is the first observed transfer since the US reinstated its blockade of Iranian ports in mid-July, said Charlie Brown, an adviser to UANI. The group based its analysis on satellite images and ship-tracking data. The US military issued a notice on Wednesday that it was widening the scope of its blockade to target ships receiving cargoes at sea. The American operation has brought Iranian oil exports to a halt , forcing production curbs and cutting off a key source of revenue for the Islamic Republic. Read More: Iran’s Main Oil Terminals Remain Empty as US Blockade Bites Some small shipments of Iranian liquefied petroleum gas have left the Middle East since the blockade was reinstated, but Brown said it’s unlikely the crude loaded onto Hao Fan is destined for global markets. The vessel took about 200,000 barrels in the ship-to-ship transfer, too little to make an export voyage economic, he added. “Things have been consistent so far with regard to the blockade,” said Brown. The timing of the US notice and the transfer between Olym and Hao Fan was likely a “happy coincidence,” but the Iranians are expected to try “all kinds of ways to get things out,” he added. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.body: Tidal & Wave Energy November 20, 2026 · 1 minute ago 1 MW floating wave energy converter gets green light for test site deployment NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email EMEC WEDUSEA, a €19.6 million collaborative project bringing together 14 European partners, has secured a marine license that allows the installation of a 1 MW OE Buoy floating wave energy converter and associated moorings at the European Marine Energy Centre's (EMEC) test site in Orkney. Co-funded by the EU Horizon Europe Programme and Innovate UK, WEDUSEA, which brings together 14 partners from industry and academia across Ireland, the UK, France, Germany and Spain, aims to create a step change for the wave energy industry and support its progression towards commercialization. The marine license granted by the Marine Directorate, previously Marine Scotland, allows the 1 MW-rated, unmanned floating oscillating water column device, developed by OceanEnergy, to be deployed at EMEC. Its only moving part, the turbine rotor, sits on deck above the waves, while all electrical equipment is housed below deck in a sealed machine room. As waves cause air trapped within the OE Buoy hull to oscillate, the airflow drives the turbine to generate electricity. This electricity will be exported to the grid via an underwater umbilical and export cable, EMEC explained. The OE Buoy and its mooring system will be installed at Berth 5 at the Billia Croo wave energy test site. Furthermore, EMEC has developed an extensive environmental monitoring plan for the deployment, which will monitor the habitat above and below the water’s surface in the vicinity of the OE Buoy. The monitoring program will begin before installation to establish a baseline of benthic and pelagic activity in the deployment area, helping to build understanding of the marine environment before, during and following deployment. articles.body: US Coast Guard Commissions New Cutter for Caribbean Ops Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 (Credit: US Coast Guard) The U.S. Coast Guard has commissioned its newest Sentinel-class fast response cutter, USCGC Marvin Perrett (WPC 1164), during a ceremony in New Orleans, ahead of the vessel's deployment to its homeport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The commissioning ceremony took place at the Julia Street Cruise Ship Terminal, marking the cutter's official entry into active service. Following commissioning, the vessel and its crew will transit to San Juan, from where they will conduct operations across the Caribbean and the United States' southern maritime approaches. Its missions will include search and rescue, maritime law enforcement and homeland security operations. The Sentinel-class cutter is equipped with advanced maritime sensors, integrated intelligence and communications systems, and capabilities for deploying pursuit boats over the horizon. The Coast Guard said the vessel would strengthen its capacity to conduct maritime security, border protection and search and rescue missions in the region. The cutter is named after Marvin Perrett, a New Orleans native and Coast Guard veteran who operated Higgins landing craft during World War II, participating in the Normandy landings and subsequent operations in southern France and the Pacific. Perrett later received a Knight of the Legion of Honor medal from France in recognition of his wartime service.

articles.title: Nexans completes deep-water cable laying ops off Australia for Chevron
articles.summary: Nexans has completed the laying and trenching of the high-voltage dynamic cable for Chevron's Jansz-Io Compression (J-IC) project offshore...
articles.body: Cabling November 20, 2026 · 1 minute ago Nexans completes deep-water cable laying ops off Australia for Chevron NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Nexans Nexans has completed the laying and trenching of the high-voltage dynamic cable for Chevron's Jansz-Io Compression (J-IC) project offshore Western Australia. The cable-laying vessel (CLV) Nexans Aurora installed 26 buoyancy modules and trenched 30 kilometers of cable, after which it left Australia on October 23. J-IC uses subsea compression to sustain gas supply to the Gorgon LNG and domestic gas plants on Barrow Island. The 145 kV cable, about 135 kilometers long, runs from the island to a floating field control station, which powers and controls the compressors on the seabed. The completed operation included the overboarding and pull-in of the cable head to the field control station, installation of the buoyancy modules using a horizontal method developed, laying of the cable in its dynamic configuration, installation of about 200 meters of vortex-induced vibration (VIV) strakes in the Scarp section, cable lay up the Scarp, float-out and pull-in of the second cable end at Barrow Island, as-laid survey and cable trenching. Before handover, the remaining work includes cable jointing at the field control station and on Barrow Island, rock stabilization along the last 28 kilometers of the route, and final soak test, planned for February. Nexans Chevron sanctioned the Jansz-Io compression project in early July 2021 and ordered the field control station from the Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering (DSME) shipyard, now known as Hanwha Ocean, a few months later. articles.title: Lufthansa Cargo adds Rome–Tel Aviv freight capacity with Poste Air Cargo
articles.summary: Lufthansa Cargo has expanded its air freight services between Rome and Tel Aviv through a new capacity agreement with Poste Air Cargo. The additional direct flights operate every Monday and Thursday from Rome-Fiumicino Airport. They are served by Boeing 737-800BCF freighters, each offering approximately 22 metric...
articles.body: Lufthansa Cargo has expanded its air freight services between Rome and Tel Aviv through a new capacity agreement with Poste Air Cargo. The additional direct flights operate every Monday and Thursday from Rome-Fiumicino Airport. They are served by Boeing 737-800BCF freighters, each offering approximately 22 metric tons of cargo capacity. Under the arrangement, Lufthansa Cargo uses capacity provided by Poste Air Cargo, the cargo airline of Italy’s Poste Italiane Group. The additional flights respond to continued demand for air freight capacity on the route. They also give customers in Italy more options for scheduling shipments to Tel Aviv. Rome hub gains additional freighter connections The new services complement Lufthansa Cargo’s existing cooperation with ITA Airways. Since June 2025, Lufthansa Cargo has gradually expanded its marketing of cargo capacity on ITA Airways flights, strengthening Rome’s role in its Southern European network. The agreement with Poste Air Cargo adds dedicated freighter capacity alongside the cargo space available on passenger aircraft. “With the additional cargo routes from Poste Air Cargo out of Rome, we are creating more capacity on a highly sought-after route and greater flexibility for shipment planning,” said Ashwin Bhat, CEO of Lufthansa Cargo. “At the same time, we are further developing Rome as a hub in Southern Europe: We are strategically supplementing ITA Airways’ cargo capacity with freighter services, thereby aligning our offerings even more closely with our customers’ needs,” Bhat added. Lufthansa Cargo expects the additional capacity to remain available for at least the rest of the winter flight schedule. Poste Air Cargo operates domestic and international cargo services, including scheduled flights, charters and ACMI operations. Its domestic network also supports mail and parcel transportation for the Poste Italiane Group.

articles.body: Europe Offshore Subsea 7 seeks buyer for pipelay vessel ahead of Saipem merger Bojan Lepic November 20, 2026 0 0 1 minute read Norwegian offshore engineering contractor Subsea 7 has begun identifying a buyer for its pipelay and heavy-lift vessel Seven Borealis , which it must divest as part of its planned merger with Saipem. The company confirmed the move in its third-quarter results, after Brazil’s competition authority, CADE, conditionally approved the merger earlier this month. The regulator required the disposal of Seven Borealis to address competition concerns in Brazil’s offshore engineering, procurement, construction, and installation market, where both contractors have a substantial presence. Subsea 7 said the vessel would be sold under an arrangement that allows it to continue fulfilling existing project commitments through a sale-and-leaseback structure. Those commitments currently extend into 2028. The company has not identified a prospective buyer or disclosed an asking price for the vessel. The planned merger will create Saipem 7, combining two of the world’s largest offshore construction contractors. Subsea 7 said 13 of the 16 relevant competition authorities have approved the transaction. Reviews remain underway in Australia, the EU, and West Africa, with completion now expected in early 2027. The Seven Borealis disposal remains a condition of the Brazilian approval. articles.body: TEN, Ltd. Reports Record Profits for the Nine Months and Third Quarter of 2026 in Hellenic Shipping News 20/11/2026 TEN, Ltd. reported results (unaudited) for the nine months and the third quarter ended September 30, 2026. NINE MONTHS 2026 SUMMARY RESULTS During the first nine months of 2026, TEN, with an average in-the-water fleet of 63 vessels, generated gross revenues of $851 million, a near $274 million increase from the nine months of 2025. The resulting net income for the first nine-months of 2026 reached $403 million equivalent to $12.69 per share compared to $2.75 per share in the nine-month period of 2025, representing a gross increase of 355%. Operating income during the 2026 nine-month period and inclusive of a $94 million capital gain from the sale of four vessels, rose to $467 million from $171 million in the corresponding period of 2025, which also included capital gains of $12.5 million. Adjusted EBITDA for the first nine months of 2026 was at $510 million from $289 million in the first nine months of 2025. Despite having 12 vessels on scheduled dry dock, one vessel undergoing repairs and some on repositing voyages during the first nine months of 2026, fleet utilization remained high at 95.5%. The average Time Charter Equivalent (TCE) rate per vessel per day for the nine months of 2026 rose to $45,170, compared with $30,703 in the nine months of 2025, representing a 47% increase, reflecting the continued strength of the tanker markets. Total operating expenses per vessel per day remained at a still competitive $10,664 in the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Depreciation and amortization in the nine months ended September 30, 2026, totaled $135 million from $126 million in the corresponding 2025 period, attributable to the operation of a slightly larger fleet consisting of newer and larger class vessels. TEN’s cash balances at the end of September 2026, stood at a healthy $533.5 million, $269 million higher than the cash levels at the end of September 2025 Total bank debt as of September 30, 2026, was $2.0 billion from $1.8 billion at September 30, 2025, reflecting new loans associated with vessels entering the fleet. Interest and finance costs for the first nine months of 2026 amounted to $65.7 million, about $7.0 million lower than the level recorded in the first nine-months of 2025, as a result of decreased spreads attained from banks for new or refinanced loans and lower global interest rates. Interest income rose to f $10.4 million in the 2026 nine-month period compared to $7.7 million received in the 2025 nine-month period. Q3 2026 SUMMARY RESULTS With an average fleet of 63 vessels, TEN’s gross revenues during the third quarter of 2026 approximated $300 million, an increase of $113 million, or 61%, over the corresponding 2025 period. Net income in the third quarter of 2026 reached $174.5 million (inclusive of the capital gains mentioned above), equivalent to $5.57 per share, from $1.05 per share in the third quarter of 2025 which also recorded the aforementioned capital gains. A 431% increase. Operating income during the third quarter of 2026, inclusive of $56.2 million capital gain from the sale of three vessels in the summer of 2026, settled at $194.5 million from $60.5 million in the equivalent quarter of 2025, which included capital gains of $8.9 million obtained from the sale of three vessels Adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter of 2026 was at $185.4 million, 94% higher from the 2025 third quarter level. Average TCE rate per vessel per day in the third quarter of 2026 reached $48,615, 59% higher than the 2025 equivalent period, supported by high fleet utilization rates of nearly 94%. Operating expenses per vessel per day in the third quarter of 2026 were $11,394. Depreciation and amortization expenses during the third quarter of 2026 were in line with the increased number of vessels in the fleet at $44.8 million, just $2.3 million higher than the 2025 third quarter levels. Consistent with the first nine-months trend, interest and finance costs in the third quarter of 2026 decreased by $1.4 million from the corresponding 2025 period to $22.3 million, benefiting from lower borrowing spreads and lower global interest rates, while interest income totaled $4.8 million. SUBSEQUENT EVENTS & OTHERS On September 29, 2026, TEN exercised its right to repurchase the 2022-built LNG carrier Tenergy, currently under a five-year finance lease, at a significant discount to fair market value. The acquisition will be completed upon the expiration of the lease in January 2027 and will be financed in its entirety through funds obtained from an international banking institution on attractive terms. On October 26, 2026, TEN announced its authorization to commence an up to $150 million buyback program covering both common and preferred shares. The timing of any share purchases of any type, the prices and the exact number of shares to be purchased will depend on prevailing market conditions, cash balances and other uses of capital. TEN is evaluating the possibility of applying to list its common shares on the Main Board of the Singapore Exchange Securities Trading Limited (the “SGX-ST”). TEN’s common shares are currently listed and traded on the New York Stock Exchange (“NYSE”) and would continue to be primarily listed and traded on NYSE. No final decision or commitment has been made as to the timing, terms or conditions of any such listing on the SGX-ST. CORPORATE AFFAIRS On October 26, 2026, TEN announced a doubling of its first 2027 semi-annual common stock dividend to $1.00 per share, up from $0.50 per share in the 2026 comparable period. The dividend is scheduled for payment on January 20, 2027, to shareholders of record as of January 12, 2027. For the entire 2026, TEN paid common shareholders a total of $1.50 per share in dividends. Since the Company’s NYSE listing in 2002, TEN has consistently demonstrated its commitment to reward shareholders, and will have distributed, until the end of 2026 over $1.0 billion in aggregate common and preferred share dividends. The Company’s 9.25% Series E Preferred Shares become redeemable at the election of the Company on May 28, 2027, and the Company currently expects that it may elect to redeem, all or a portion of, such Series E Preferred Shares on the above stated date. This disclosure does not constitute a notice of redemption, and there can be no assurance as to the amount, if any, of the Series E Preferred Shares that will be redeemed. CORPORATE STRATEGY As tanker market fundamentals, in terms of supply and demand remain healthy and continue to be supported by trade dislocations stemming from geopolitics, TEN benefits from the very strong conditions evident both in the freight market and the firm asset values. Accordingly, TEN continues to capture the market upside through spot and profit-sharing contracts, while pursuing long-term charter coverage at today’s high levels. With cash balances well in excess of half a billion dollars, and $3.6 billion of future revenues, management remains committed to evaluating accretive growth opportunities across the various sectors in which TEN operates, while continuing to focus on the divestment of older assets where demand remains strong. “TEN is navigating through this unprecedented environment with a diversified and high-quality fleet, positioned to capture market upside by securing firm forward revenues and providing shareholders with attractive returns. In parallel, it is continuing its dynamic 20-vessel newbuilding program,” stated Mr. George Saroglou, COO and President of TEN. “The doubling of the 2027 first semi-annual dividend, the $150 million buyback program together with the divestment of older tonnage highlights management’s intention to use TEN’s healthy and growing cash balances for the long-term benefit of the Company, and its shareholders,” To this end, and having been pioneers in the capital markets with a first public listing back in 1993 on the Oslo Bors, and in 2002 on the NYSE, management currently evaluates a possible secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange (SGX), in order to position the Company in the growing Asian capital market going forward” Mr. Saroglou concluded. articles.title: Decision time on carbon pricing for global shipping at the UN
articles.summary: Governments are set to decide on the future of the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) for global shipping, a landmark climate agreement introducing the world’s first global carbon pricing on any industry. The negotiations are planned to take place at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) as a three-part summit:...
articles.body: Decision time on carbon pricing for global shipping at the UN in International Shipping News 20/11/2026 Governments are set to decide on the future of the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) for global shipping, a landmark climate agreement introducing the world’s first global carbon pricing on any industry. The negotiations are planned to take place at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) as a three-part summit: technical working group talks (ISWG-GHG-23) on 23-27 November, the 85th session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) on 30 November – 3 December, and potentially the Extraordinary Session (MEPC E.2) on 4 December. The talks will decide the fate of ~5% of global oil demand represented by global shipping, making the stakes for energy security and climate extremely high. The meeting is also a test whether global “middle powers” can unite despite the US and other petro states and deliver meaningful global climate action this year. Discussions in the first week (ISWG-GHG-23) will primarily focus on the NZF’s key elements, such as the agreed limits to phase-out fossil fuels, clean energy and carbon pricing revenues, and whether any possible changes can deliver a compromise that works for all countries, including climate champions as well as persistent opponents of climate action. Political discussions in the second week (MEPC85) are likely to culminate in a decision on the adoption of the Framework, either in its current form or with possible changes, on Friday 4 December. Latest evidence from UCL and RMI shows that the NZF in its current form is the best, most cost-effective way for the industry to achieve its climate commitments under the 2023 Revised Strategy. Experts warn further delaying the NZF adoption would accelerate the rise of national and regional rules, which are already emerging in Africa and Europe, resulting in a regulatory patchwork unable to provide the unanimity and predictability that global trade requires. The IMO discussions follow the COP 31 Climate Summit putting a spotlight on shipping action. Over 110 maritime companies and industry associations called on the IMO Member States to adopt the NZF this year. Over 30 maritime organizations committed to increasing electricity’s share of shipping’s energy use to at least 20% by 2035, stating that a strong global policy at the IMO is necessary to help achieve this goal. Em Fenton, Senior Director, Climate Diplomacy, Opportunity Green says: “We have seen real solidarity and progress at shipping’s climate negotiations over the past two years. Now it’s crunch time and we cannot allow those who shout the loudest to pull the rug out from under the table. Climate vulnerable countries have fought hard for a plan to decarbonise the shipping sector, and waited long enough to see this put into action. Now, Member States must adopt a Net-Zero Framework that cleans up the global shipping industry in a way that supports communities facing the worst impacts of the climate crisis and ensures that everyone pays a fair price for their shipping pollution.” Alex Springer, Deputy Director of Shipping, Transport & Environment, said: “The biggest danger at MEPC 85 is no longer delay, but a rushed deal designed to get Trump and his allies to the table. Carving out an indefinite transition to fossil LNG and crop biofuels is not progress; it would be a concession to US and Saudi business interests and will prolong shipping’s fossil fuel dependency at the expense of climate action. IMO member states, in the EU and elsewhere, must resist pressure to reach a deal at any cost that would simply swap the industry from one set of dirty fuels to another.” Delaine McCullough, Shipping Program Director, Ocean Conservancy, said: “Adopting the agreed upon Net-Zero Framework is the quickest and most effective way to protect communities, address climate change, and create certainty for the shipping industry for decades to come. As this year’s stunning weather disasters make clear, our ocean and the industry cannot afford to kick the hard decisions down the road again.” Lucas Leppert, President, the Clean Shipping Coalition, said: “In the more than 12 months delay in adoption of the NZF, the world has seen increased climate impacts: floods, droughts, heatwaves, and wildfires. There is no longer time for going in circles; every IMO member state must get behind the Net-Zero Framework and adopt it before the year ends.” Jesse Fahnestock, Director of Decarbonisation, Global Maritime Forum, said: “As we approach the critical meetings of the next two weeks, the space for agreement is narrowing. Further delay or weakening of agreed elements risks costly delays and abandonment of investments by first movers, and would likely drive further regulatory fragmentation to fill the ambition gap. Global shipping needs two things first and foremost: a credible, sufficient, and transparently-managed price signal, and a predictable, fixed trajectory for emissions reductions. Amongst the options discussed, the NZF is the one that delivers on that.” Davina Hurt, Climate Policy Director, Pacific Environment, said: “For generations, communities living near ports have carried the burden of shipping pollution — in their children’s lungs, in their homes and in their shortened lives. Meanwhile, islands and coastal communities that have done the least to cause the climate crisis, are watching the sea take their land. The Net-Zero Framework now on the table is our best chance in a generation to step toward cleaner fuels and move towards a more equitable solution. It’s time to finally put the costs where they belong: on polluters and the fossil fuel companies that continue to make billions in profits each year. Member states should ensure that a funding mechanism delivers for those communities who need it the most. Delegates can not afford to walk away from this responsibility again.” Adria Jover, President & Founder, International Electric Maritime Association (IEMA), says: “At COP31, we witnessed an unprecedented alignment of industry and NGO voices demanding the rapid electrification of the global fleet and ports worldwide. The responsibility to turn this pledge into action sits now in London. As the next round of IMO meetings begins, the adoption of the Net-Zero Framework is the first and most critical opportunity for IMO Member States to show that they are hearing these voices and send the definitive market signal the industry needs to electrify at scale.” Sandra Moguel, Legal Research & Coordination Lead, Equal Routes, said: “As negotiations resume at the IMO, Member States will decide how the Net-Zero Framework treats LNG and other methane-based fuels. LNG can look cleaner on paper than it is in practice, because methane that slips through engines or leaks along the supply chain is easy to miss. It should not receive rewards without fully accounting for that slip and leakage on a well-to-wake basis. This is the moment to give every delegation equal access to the information shaping these talks, so no decision rests on incomplete data or assumptions.” Emily Zhang, Analyst at InfluenceMap, said: “We’re seeing broad corporate support for the Net-Zero Framework across shipping and fuels, from major carriers to associations representing most of the world’s fleet. But that support doesn’t extend to every detail. Ahead of the framework’s approval, some of the same groups pushed for a lower carbon price and a weaker fuel standard, which would pull the framework away from the net-zero trajectory IMO members set in the 2023 GHG Strategy. Oil and gas groups have also lobbied for accounting rules that would make fossil fuels count as cleaner. As IMO member states reconvene, the test is whether they adopt the framework as agreed, or let it be weakened in the fine print.” Aurelia Leeuw, Director of EU Policy, SASHA Coalition, said: “Industry is united in asking for action – shipping companies, ports and maritime businesses need global regulatory clarity so they can direct investment away from fossil fuels. It’s time for IMO Member States to hear these calls and finally adopt a Net-Zero Framework that will support the most truly sustainable fuels and technologies of the future. Europe must continue to push for an outcome that creates predictable investment signals that are urgently needed for a sustainable future for international shipping.” The NZF combines gradually more strict carbon intensity targets with carbon pricing. The mechanism was agreed at the IMO in April 2025 by an overwhelming majority. The adoption was delayed a few months later, in a close vote (57 in favour and 49 against) in October 2025, due to strong pressure from the US, Saudi Arabia and other petro states. The IMO agreed to discuss adoption again at the end of 2026. articles.title: LR approves new Rules for nuclear-powered ships and offshore units

articles.body: LR approves new Rules for nuclear-powered ships and offshore units in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 20/11/2026 Lloyd’s Register (LR) has approved Rules for the Classification of Ships and Offshore Units Integrated with Nuclear Power, providing a common classification framework to support the assessment of nuclear technologies for maritime use. They are believed to be the first Rules developed by a class society that are suitable for all types of ship and offshore units. The Rules have been approved by LR’s Ships and Offshore Technical Committees and will evolve as nuclear maritime technologies mature. Interest in nuclear power for maritime use is gathering momentum, with governments, regulators, shipowners and technology developers increasingly working together to address practical barriers to deployment. The new Rules respond to growing demand for guidance on the practical steps needed to bring nuclear power into maritime applications. Claudene Sharp-Patel, Global Technical Director, Lloyd’s Register Reactor agnostic, the Rules are underpinned by goals and functional requirements, an approach intended to accommodate different nuclear technologies and marine applications as designs and international regulation continue to evolve. They will form part of a wider suite of classification and Advisory tools to support the development of nuclear maritime projects, which will be announced separately. Claudene Sharp-Patel, Global Technical Director at LR, said: “The maritime industry needs a clear classification framework to assess how advanced nuclear technologies can be integrated into ships and offshore units. These Rules set out the goals to be achieved, the functions to be performed and the evidence needed to demonstrate that a design meets the requirements, without prescribing a particular reactor technology.” The framework draws on LR’s risk-based certification (RBC) process to help align maritime requirements with nuclear licensing, using the same goal-based approach in the nuclear Rules. Mark Tipping, Global Offshore Power-to-X Director at LR, said: “The opportunity for nuclear in maritime extends well beyond ship power. From nuclear-powered vessels to floating power units and reliable, low-carbon energy for ports and neighbouring industries, there is potential to reshape how the sector produces and uses energy. “These rules provide a common framework for those developing or bringing forward nuclear maritime projects.” Mark Tipping, Global Offshore Power-to-X Director, Lloyd’s Register Nuclear’s high energy density brings the potential for long intervals between refuelling and reliable power for propulsion and onboard services, reducing reliance on conventional bunker fuel supplies. Inherently safe, it supports greater flexibility in vessel deployment, while avoiding greenhouse gas emissions during operation. The Rules form part of LR’s wider work to support the safe deployment of advanced nuclear technology in maritime. This includes Advisory support on feasibility and integration risks, contributions to international regulatory development through the Nuclear Energy Maritime Organization (NEMO) and work with the British Ports Association on a practical readiness pathway for ports considering nuclear-powered ships and floating nuclear power units. LR’s expertise spans voyage, vessel and people, combining classification, Advisory and digital providing the Power of Three to assess nuclear technologies, understand integration risks and make informed decisions on maritime applications. takeaways: They are believed to be the first Rules developed by a class society that are suitable for all types of ship and offshore units.
The Rules have been approved by LR’s Ships and Offshore Technical Committees and will evolve as nuclear maritime technologies mature.

Interest in nuclear power for maritime use is gathering momentum, with governments, regulators, shipowners and technology developers increasingly working together to address practical barriers to deployment.

The new management arrangement took effect on 1 November 2026. It follows Lufthansa Cargo’s move to take full ownership of the German air cargo handling company earlier this month. New leadership follows Lufthansa Cargo acquisition The management changes come as Lufthansa Cargo strengthens its ground handling operations in Germany. The company signed an agreement to acquire LUG in September 2026 and completed the acquisition in early November. The transaction is intended to increase handling capacity and support the airline’s long-term growth plans. “With Patrik Tschirch and Uwe Glunz, we have a strong and experienced leadership team at the helm of LUG,” said Frank Bauer, Chief Operating Officer, Lufthansa Cargo. “Together, they will continue the company’s successful growth and further strengthen LUG’s position as the top choice in air cargo handling,” Bauer added. The new leadership team will oversee LUG’s operations as the company enters its next phase under Lufthansa Cargo’s ownership.

The development forms part of the wider Berwick Bank offshore wind complex, which has a proposed capacity of approximately 4.1GW. The Berwick Bank B agreement remains subject to final contract award and SSE’s final investment decision, expected in late 2027. Subject to approval, preparatory offshore construction could begin in 2028, with foundation and cable installation continuing into 2031. Seaway 7 previously worked with SSE on the Beatrice and Seagreen offshore wind farms.
